expectedText:
DISSENTERS' RIGHTS (APPRAISAL RIGHTS) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE — DISSENTERS' RIGHTS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet relates to Acme, Inc., a stock corporation organized under the laws of California, and to Jordan Lee's status as a shareholder of Acme, Inc. holding 1,000 shares of common stock, in connection with the following corporate transaction: Merger of Acme, Inc. into Beta Holdings, Inc. It describes the dissenters' rights (sometimes called appraisal rights) that Cal. Corp. Code §§ 1300-1313 -- Chapter 13 of the General Corporation Law, titled "Dissenters' Rights" -- give a shareholder of a California corporation who dissents from certain reorganizations requiring outstanding-share approval under Section 1201, from a short-form merger, or from a conversion treated as a reorganization under Section 1313, to require the corporation to purchase the shareholder's dissenting shares for cash at fair market value rather than accept whatever consideration the transaction otherwise provides.

This information sheet is educational only. It does not itself constitute a written demand on Acme, Inc. under Section 1301, does not determine whether Jordan Lee's shares meet the statutory definition of "dissenting shares" in Section 1300(b) for Merger of Acme, Inc. into Beta Holdings, Inc., does not determine whether the "market-out" exception described below removes or preserves dissenters' rights for any specific shares, and does not calculate the fair market value of any specific shares.

WHAT DISSENTERS' RIGHTS ARE, AND THE TRANSACTIONS THAT TRIGGER THEM
California's General Corporation Law gives a shareholder of a corporation a statutory right to "dissent" from certain reorganizations and demand cash instead of whatever the reorganization otherwise provides. Specifically, if outstanding-share approval of a corporation is required for a reorganization under particular subdivisions of Section 1201, each shareholder of that corporation entitled to vote on the transaction -- and each shareholder of a subsidiary corporation in a short-form merger -- may, by complying with the dissenters'-rights chapter's procedure, require the corporation in which the shareholder holds shares to purchase for cash, at fair market value, the shares owned by the shareholder that qualify as "dissenting shares." This right is not limited to mergers and asset-reorganization transactions structured as corporate reorganizations in the first instance: a conversion of a corporation into a different business-entity type is itself deemed to constitute a reorganization for purposes of this same chapter, so a shareholder facing a conversion can likewise have dissenters' rights, to the extent the conversion statute provides.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "If the approval of the outstanding shares (Section 152) of a corporation is required for a reorganization under subdivisions (a) and (b) or subdivision (e) or (f) of Section 1201, each shareholder of the corporation entitled to vote on the transaction and each shareholder of a subsidiary corporation in a short-form merger may, by complying with this chapter, require the corporation in which the shareholder holds shares to purchase for cash at their fair market value the shares owned by the shareholder which are dissenting shares as defined in subdivision (b)."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1300(a), California General Corporation Law, Chapter 13 ("Dissenters' Rights"), the right to demand cash purchase of dissenting shares (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1300.)
  "A conversion pursuant to Chapter 11.5 (commencing with Section 1150) shall be deemed to constitute a reorganization for purposes of applying the provisions of this chapter, in accordance with and to the extent provided in Section 1159."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1313, California General Corporation Law, dissenters'-rights chapter extended to certain entity conversions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1313.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine, defined shareholder right -- not a claim about which state's law would apply to a specific corporation, and not a claim that every jurisdiction's appraisal-rights statute works the same way. The two citations below (Cal. Corp. Code § 1300(a) and Cal. Corp. Code § 1313) are drawn from two separately, independently numbered sections of the dissenters'-rights chapter, so they are treated as independent sources of that chapter's own scope. Section 1300(a) itself cross-references "subdivisions (a) and (b) or subdivision (e) or (f) of Section 1201" as the specific reorganizations that trigger the right, and separately cross-references the short-form merger procedure; this document quotes that cross-reference as it appears in Section 1300's own text, but Section 1201's substantive definitions of those reorganization subdivisions were not independently fetched and confirmed twice for this document, so this document does not itself catalog which specific transaction structures fall within subdivisions (a), (b), (e), or (f) of Section 1201. This document also does not determine whether a specific proposed transaction is a reorganization requiring outstanding-share approval, whether a specific shareholder is "entitled to vote on the transaction," or whether a specific conversion triggers dissenters' rights under Section 1313's cross-reference to Section 1159 (which was likewise not independently verified here).

THE "MARKET-OUT" EXCEPTION FOR LISTED SHARES, AND ITS CARVE-BACKS
California's dissenters'-rights statute does not give every shareholder of a corporation involved in a qualifying reorganization the right to demand a cash purchase; a share loses eligibility as a "dissenting share" if, immediately before the reorganization or short-form merger, it was listed on a national securities exchange certified by the Commissioner of Financial Protection and Innovation under Section 25100(o), and the notice of the shareholders' meeting summarized the dissenters'-rights statutes -- this is the "market-out" exception. That exception is narrower than a blanket rule against dissenters' rights for all listed shares, in two distinct ways. First, it does not apply at all to shares subject to any restriction on transfer imposed by the corporation or by any law or regulation, regardless of listing status. Second, and independently, it does not apply to any shares whose holder is required by the terms of the reorganization or short-form merger to accept anything other than (A) shares of another corporation that are themselves listed on a certified national exchange when the transaction becomes effective, (B) cash in lieu of fractional shares of that listed stock, or (C) a combination of (A) and (B) -- meaning a listed shareholder who will be cashed out, or paid in unlisted securities or debt, keeps dissenters' rights even though the shareholder's own stock was listed. A separate and textually distinct exclusion, resting on the share's own contractual terms rather than its trading market, removes an entire class of shares from most of the dissenters'-rights chapter (though not from the chapter's provision limiting other remedies) when that class's own terms and provisions specifically state what its holders are to be paid in a reorganization or merger.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "That were not, immediately prior to the reorganization or short-form merger, listed on any national securities exchange certified by the Commissioner of Financial Protection and Innovation under subdivision (o) of Section 25100, and the notice of meeting of shareholders to act upon the reorganization summarizes this section and Sections 1301, 1302, 1303, and 1304; provided, however, that this provision does not apply to any shares with respect to which there exists any restriction on transfer imposed by the corporation or by any law or regulation; and provided, further, that this provision does not apply to any shares where the holder of those shares is required, by the terms of the reorganization or short-form merger, to accept for the shares anything except: (A) shares of any other corporation, which shares, at the time the reorganization or short-form merger is effective, are listed on any national securities exchange certified by the Commissioner of Financial Protection and Innovation under subdivision (o) of Section 25100; (B) cash in lieu of fractional shares described in the foregoing subparagraph (A); or (C) any combination of the shares and cash in lieu of fractional shares described in the foregoing subparagraphs (A) and (B)."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1300(b)(1), California General Corporation Law, "market-out" exception excluding certain listed shares from the definition of dissenting shares (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1300.)
  "This chapter, except Section 1312, does not apply to classes of shares whose terms and provisions specifically set forth the amount to be paid in respect to such shares in the event of a reorganization or merger."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1311, California General Corporation Law, separate exclusion for share classes with contractually specified reorganization payment terms (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1311.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual, narrower scope of this exception -- not a claim about which state's law would apply to a specific corporation, and not a claim that every jurisdiction's market-out rule has the same carve-backs. It is worth stating precisely because it corrects a natural assumption: the market-out exception is not a blanket denial of dissenters' rights whenever a shareholder's stock happens to be exchange-listed. It applies only when the reorganization's notice of meeting summarized the dissenters'-rights statutes, and even then it is defeated (i.e., dissenters' rights survive) if there is any transfer restriction on the shares, or if the consideration the shareholder must accept is anything other than listed stock of the acquirer (plus cash only for fractional shares). This document does not independently confirm which specific exchanges are currently certified by the Commissioner of Financial Protection and Innovation under Section 25100(o), and does not determine whether a specific corporation's shares were listed on such an exchange immediately before a specific transaction, or whether a specific transaction's notice of meeting in fact summarized the required statutes. The two citations below are drawn from two separately, independently numbered sections (Cal. Corp. Code § 1300(b)(1) and Cal. Corp. Code § 1311); within Section 1300(b)(1) itself, no second independent source was located or used to further corroborate that specific subdivision's text beyond the two independent fetches of Section 1300 described in this document's overall verification record. Section 1311's contractual-terms exclusion described here is a separate exception from the market-out rule -- it turns on a share class's own stated redemption or payment terms, not on whether the shares are exchange-listed -- and this document does not address how the two exceptions interact if both could apply to the same shares.

PROCEDURAL STEPS AND DEADLINES TO DEMAND PURCHASE
A shareholder who wants the corporation to purchase the shareholder's shares for cash must make a written demand on the corporation for the purchase and for payment of their fair market value in cash. That demand is not effective for any purpose unless the corporation or its transfer agent receives it by a statutory deadline: not later than the date of the shareholders' meeting to vote on the reorganization, for shares described in Section 1300(b); or, in any other case, within 30 days after the date the corporation mailed the shareholder its notice of the outstanding-share approval, or the notice required under Section 1110(h). The written demand itself must state the number and class of shares of record the shareholder demands that the corporation purchase, and must state what the shareholder claims to be the shares' fair market value -- which itself operates as an offer by the shareholder to sell at that stated price. Separately from making that demand, and within the same 30-day window measured from the mailed notice, the shareholder must also submit the shares for endorsement: for certificated shares, submitting the certificates to the corporation or its transfer agent to be stamped or endorsed as dissenting shares (or exchanged for correspondingly stamped or endorsed certificates); for uncertificated shares, submitting written notice of the number of shares the shareholder demands the corporation purchase.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "Any shareholder who has a right to require the corporation to purchase the shareholder’s shares for cash under Section 1300, subject to compliance with paragraphs (3) and (4) of subdivision (b) thereof, and who desires the corporation to purchase shares shall make written demand upon the corporation for the purchase of those shares and payment to the shareholder in cash of their fair market value. The demand is not effective for any purpose unless it is received by the corporation or any transfer agent thereof (1) in the case of shares described in subdivision (b) of Section 1300, not later than the date of the shareholders’ meeting to vote upon the reorganization, or (2) in any other case, within 30 days after the date on which the notice of the approval by the outstanding shares pursuant to subdivision (a) or the notice pursuant to subdivision (h) of Section 1110 was mailed to the shareholder."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1301(b)-(c), California General Corporation Law, written demand for purchase of dissenting shares and its statutory deadline (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1301.)
  "Within 30 days after the date on which notice of the approval by the outstanding shares or the notice pursuant to subdivision (h) of Section 1110 was mailed to the shareholder, the shareholder shall submit to the corporation at its principal office or at the office of any transfer agent thereof, (a) if the shares are certificated securities, the shareholder’s certificates representing any shares which the shareholder demands that the corporation purchase, to be stamped or endorsed with a statement that the shares are dissenting shares or to be exchanged for certificates of appropriate denomination so stamped or endorsed or (b) if the shares are uncertificated securities, written notice of the number of shares which the shareholder demands that the corporation purchase."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1302, California General Corporation Law, deadline and method for submitting dissenting shares for endorsement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1302.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual procedural steps and deadlines -- not a claim about which state's law would apply to a specific corporation, and not a claim that every jurisdiction's appraisal procedure works the same way. The two citations below are drawn from two separately, independently numbered sections (Cal. Corp. Code § 1301(b)-(c) and Cal. Corp. Code § 1302). This document quotes, but does not resolve, an ambiguity in Section 1301(b)(1)'s own text: it ties the meeting-date deadline to "shares described in subdivision (b) of Section 1300," which is the same subdivision that defines dissenting shares generally (including, in its own text, a proviso about written-consent approval versus a shareholders' meeting) -- this document does not independently determine exactly which demands fall under the meeting-date track versus the 30-day-after-mailed-notice track beyond what each section's own text states, and a specific shareholder's applicable deadline depends on the specific transaction's approval method and notice. This document also does not calculate or confirm any specific deadline date for a specific transaction, and does not itself constitute the written demand or submission for endorsement that Sections 1301 and 1302 describe.

HOW FAIR MARKET VALUE IS DETERMINED, AND WHEN PAYMENT IS DUE
The statute fixes both the valuation date and the valuation method for dissenting shares: fair market value is determined as of the day of, and immediately prior to, the first announcement of the terms of the proposed reorganization or short-form merger, excluding any appreciation or depreciation that results from the proposed transaction itself, and as adjusted for any stock split, reverse stock split, or share dividend that becomes effective after that date. If the corporation and the shareholder agree that the shares are dissenting shares and agree on a price, the shareholder is entitled to that agreed price plus interest at the legal rate on judgments running from the date of the agreement, and the agreement fixing fair market value must be filed with the corporation's secretary. Once fair market value is set (by agreement, or otherwise as described elsewhere in this chapter), payment is due within 30 days after the amount is agreed, or within 30 days after any statutory or contractual conditions to the reorganization are satisfied, whichever is later, and -- for certificated shares -- payment is subject to surrender of the certificates unless the parties agree otherwise.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "The fair market value shall be determined as of the day of, and immediately prior to, the first announcement of the terms of the proposed reorganization or short-form merger, excluding any appreciation or depreciation in consequence of the proposed reorganization or short-form merger, as adjusted for any stock split, reverse stock split, or share dividend that becomes effective thereafter."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1300(a), California General Corporation Law, valuation date and method for dissenting shares' fair market value (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1300.)
  "If the corporation and the shareholder agree that the shares are dissenting shares and agree upon the price of the shares, the dissenting shareholder is entitled to the agreed price with interest thereon at the legal rate on judgments from the date of the agreement. Any agreements fixing the fair market value of any dissenting shares as between the corporation and the holders thereof shall be filed with the secretary of the corporation. (b) Subject to the provisions of Section 1306, payment of the fair market value of dissenting shares shall be made within 30 days after the amount thereof has been agreed or within 30 days after any statutory or contractual conditions to the reorganization are satisfied, whichever is later, and in the case of certificated securities, subject to surrender of the certificates therefor, unless provided otherwise by agreement."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1303(a)-(b), California General Corporation Law, agreed price and timing of payment for dissenting shares (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1303.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual valuation date, valuation method, and payment timing -- not a claim about which state's law would apply to a specific corporation, and not a claim that every jurisdiction's appraisal statute fixes the same valuation date or measures value the same way. The two citations below are drawn from two separately, independently numbered sections (Cal. Corp. Code § 1300(a) and Cal. Corp. Code § 1303(a)-(b)). This document does not describe the separate mechanism (Section 1306, not independently verified for this document) under which unpaid fair market value can become a subordinated debt of the corporation if a distributions-restriction statute prevents payment, and it does not calculate the fair market value, the applicable legal rate of interest, or any specific payment date for any specific shares or transaction.

COURT ACTION TO RESOLVE DISPUTED STATUS OR VALUE, AND HOW COSTS ARE ALLOCATED
If the corporation denies that particular shares are dissenting shares, or if the corporation and the shareholder cannot agree on fair market value, the shareholder demanding purchase (or any interested corporation) may file a complaint in the superior court of the proper county asking the court to determine whether the shares are dissenting shares, the shares' fair market value, or both -- or may intervene in a pending action raising the same questions. That complaint must be filed within six months after the date the corporation mailed its notice of outstanding-share approval, or the Section 1110(h) notice, to the shareholder; the statute states this deadline applies "but not thereafter." On the resulting trial, the court decides any disputed status issue first, and then determines fair market value itself or appoints one or more impartial appraisers to do so. Costs of that action, including reasonable compensation for court-appointed appraisers, are generally allocated as the court finds equitable; but if the appraised value exceeds the price the corporation had offered, the corporation must pay the costs, and the court has discretion to include attorneys' fees, expert-witness fees, and interest at the legal rate running from the date the shareholder complied with the demand-and-endorsement statutes, if the value the court awards for the shares turns out to be more than 125 percent of the price the corporation had offered.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "If the corporation denies that the shares are dissenting shares, or the corporation and the shareholder fail to agree upon the fair market value of the shares, then the shareholder demanding purchase of such shares as dissenting shares or any interested corporation, within six months after the date on which notice of the approval by the outstanding shares (Section 152) or notice pursuant to subdivision (h) of Section 1110 was mailed to the shareholder, but not thereafter, may file a complaint in the superior court of the proper county praying the court to determine whether the shares are dissenting shares or the fair market value of the dissenting shares or both or may intervene in any action pending on such a complaint."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1304(a), California General Corporation Law, action to determine dissenting-share status or fair market value, and its filing deadline (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1304.)
  "The costs of the action, including reasonable compensation to the appraisers to be fixed by the court, shall be assessed or apportioned as the court considers equitable, but, if the appraisal exceeds the price offered by the corporation, the corporation shall pay the costs (including in the discretion of the court attorneys’ fees, fees of expert witnesses and interest at the legal rate on judgments from the date of compliance with Sections 1300, 1301 and 1302 if the value awarded by the court for the shares is more than 125 percent of the price offered by the corporation under subdivision (a) of Section 1301)."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1305(e), California General Corporation Law, allocation of litigation costs and fee-shifting when the court's appraisal exceeds the corporation's offer (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1305.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual court-enforcement mechanism and cost-shifting rule -- not a claim about which state's law would apply to a specific corporation, and not a claim that every jurisdiction's appraisal statute allocates litigation costs the same way. The two citations below are drawn from two separately, independently numbered sections (Cal. Corp. Code § 1304(a) and Cal. Corp. Code § 1305(e)). This document does not describe the separate rules in Section 1304(b)-(c) (joinder and consolidation of multiple dissenting shareholders' claims) or Section 1305(a)-(d) (the appraisers' reporting procedure and the form of judgment) in full, and does not determine whether a specific corporation's denial of dissenting-share status, or a specific valuation dispute, would in fact be litigated in a specific county's superior court, nor does it calculate any specific award, cost allocation, or the 125 percent threshold for any specific transaction.

LOSING DISSENTING-SHARE STATUS, AND THE STATUTE'S LIMITS ON ATTACKING THE TRANSACTION ITSELF
Shares can lose their status as dissenting shares -- and their holder can cease to be entitled to require the corporation to purchase them -- in any of several ways the statute lists: if the corporation abandons the reorganization (in which case the corporation must instead pay, on demand, the good-faith dissenting shareholder's necessary expenses and reasonable attorneys' fees incurred pursuing the dissenters'-rights process); if the shares are transferred before being submitted for endorsement, or are surrendered for conversion into another class under the articles; if the shareholder and corporation fail to agree on the shares' status or price and neither side files (or intervenes in) a court action within six months after the relevant notice was mailed; or if the shareholder withdraws the demand for purchase with the corporation's consent. Separately, the dissenters'-rights chapter limits what other remedies a shareholder who holds this cash-purchase right can pursue over the underlying transaction: a shareholder with a right under this chapter to demand cash for their shares generally has no right, at law or in equity, to attack the validity of the reorganization or short-form merger, or to have it set aside or rescinded -- except in an action testing whether the required vote to authorize or approve the transaction was legally obtained. That said, a holder of a share class whose own terms specifically set out what is to be paid on a reorganization is entitled to payment under those terms.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "Dissenting shares lose their status as dissenting shares and the holders thereof cease to be dissenting shareholders and cease to be entitled to require the corporation to purchase their shares upon the happening of any of the following: (a) The corporation abandons the reorganization. Upon abandonment of the reorganization, the corporation shall pay on demand to any dissenting shareholder who has initiated proceedings in good faith under this chapter all necessary expenses incurred in such proceedings and reasonable attorneys’ fees."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1309, California General Corporation Law, events that cause shares to lose their status as dissenting shares (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1309.)
  "No shareholder of a corporation who has a right under this chapter to demand payment of cash for the shares held by the shareholder shall have any right at law or in equity to attack the validity of the reorganization or short-form merger, or to have the reorganization or short-form merger set aside or rescinded, except in an action to test whether the number of shares required to authorize or approve the reorganization have been legally voted in favor thereof; but any holder of shares of a class whose terms and provisions specifically set forth the amount to be paid in respect to them in the event of a reorganization or short-form merger is entitled to payment in accordance with those terms and provisions or, if the principal terms of the reorganization are approved pursuant to subdivision (b) of Section 1202, is entitled to payment in accordance with the terms and provisions of the approved reorganization."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1312(a), California General Corporation Law, dissenters' rights as the shareholder's limited remedy against the reorganization itself (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1312.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of both the actual triggers for losing dissenting-share status and the actual limits this chapter places on other remedies -- not a claim about which state's law would apply to a specific corporation, and not a claim that dissenters' rights are always a shareholder's exclusive remedy in every jurisdiction. The two citations below are drawn from two separately, independently numbered sections (Cal. Corp. Code § 1309 and Cal. Corp. Code § 1312(a)). This document does not restate Section 1312(b)-(c) in full (the separate rule, and burden of proof, that applies when one party to the reorganization directly or indirectly controls another party to it), and it does not determine whether a specific shareholder's shares have in fact lost dissenting-share status, or whether a specific challenge to a specific transaction falls within the narrow vote-legality exception this section preserves.

CLOSING AND SIGNATURE BLOCK — DISSENTERS' RIGHTS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet regarding Acme, Inc. was prepared by Jordan Lee.

Executed on September 1, 2026 at Oakland, California.

Signature of Jordan Lee: ☐ _________________________

It is not a completed written demand under Section 1301, does not itself preserve, waive, or exercise any dissenters' rights with respect to Acme, Inc., and does not constitute legal advice. The current statutory text is published by the California Legislative Information website (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov).]

It is worth stating precisely because it corrects a natural assumption: the market-out exception is not a blanket denial of dissenters' rights whenever a shareholder's stock happens to be exchange-listed. expectedJSON.body: A shareholder who wants the corporation to purchase the shareholder's shares for cash must make a written demand on the corporation for the purchase and for payment of their fair market value in cash. That demand is not effective for any purpose unless the corporation or its transfer agent receives it by a statutory deadline: not later than the date of the shareholders' meeting to vote on the reorganization, for shares described in Section 1300(b); or, in any other case, within 30 days after the date the corporation mailed the shareholder its notice of the outstanding-share approval, or the notice required under Section 1110(h). The written demand itself must state the number and class of shares of record the shareholder demands that the corporation purchase, and must state what the shareholder claims to be the shares' fair market value -- which itself operates as an offer by the shareholder to sell at that stated price. Separately from making that demand, and within the same 30-day window measured from the mailed notice, the shareholder must also submit the shares for endorsement: for certificated shares, submitting the certificates to the corporation or its transfer agent to be stamped or endorsed as dissenting shares (or exchanged for correspondingly stamped or endorsed certificates); for uncertificated shares, submitting written notice of the number of shares the shareholder demands the corporation purchase.

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, written demand for purchase of dissenting shares and its statutory deadline
citations.quote: Any shareholder who has a right to require the corporation to purchase the shareholder’s shares for cash under Section 1300, subject to compliance with paragraphs (3) and (4) of subdivision (b) thereof, and who desires the corporation to purchase shares shall make written demand upon the corporation for the purchase of those shares and payment to the shareholder in cash of their fair market value. The demand is not effective for any purpose unless it is received by the corporation or any transfer agent thereof (1) in the case of shares described in subdivision (b) of Section 1300, not later than the date of the shareholders’ meeting to vote upon the reorganization, or (2) in any other case, within 30 days after the date on which the notice of the approval by the outstanding shares pursuant to subdivision (a) or the notice pursuant to subdivision (h) of Section 1110 was mailed to the shareholder.

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, deadline and method for submitting dissenting shares for endorsement
citations.quote: Within 30 days after the date on which notice of the approval by the outstanding shares or the notice pursuant to subdivision (h) of Section 1110 was mailed to the shareholder, the shareholder shall submit to the corporation at its principal office or at the office of any transfer agent thereof, (a) if the shares are certificated securities, the shareholder’s certificates representing any shares which the shareholder demands that the corporation purchase, to be stamped or endorsed with a statement that the shares are dissenting shares or to be exchanged for certificates of appropriate denomination so stamped or endorsed or (b) if the shares are uncertificated securities, written notice of the number of shares which the shareholder demands that the corporation purchase.

expectedJSON.body: The statute fixes both the valuation date and the valuation method for dissenting shares: fair market value is determined as of the day of, and immediately prior to, the first announcement of the terms of the proposed reorganization or short-form merger, excluding any appreciation or depreciation that results from the proposed transaction itself, and as adjusted for any stock split, reverse stock split, or share dividend that becomes effective after that date. If the corporation and the shareholder agree that the shares are dissenting shares and agree on a price, the shareholder is entitled to that agreed price plus interest at the legal rate on judgments running from the date of the agreement, and the agreement fixing fair market value must be filed with the corporation's secretary. Once fair market value is set (by agreement, or otherwise as described elsewhere in this chapter), payment is due within 30 days after the amount is agreed, or within 30 days after any statutory or contractual conditions to the reorganization are satisfied, whichever is later, and -- for certificated shares -- payment is subject to surrender of the certificates unless the parties agree otherwise.

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, valuation date and method for dissenting shares' fair market value
citations.quote: The fair market value shall be determined as of the day of, and immediately prior to, the first announcement of the terms of the proposed reorganization or short-form merger, excluding any appreciation or depreciation in consequence of the proposed reorganization or short-form merger, as adjusted for any stock split, reverse stock split, or share dividend that becomes effective thereafter.

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, agreed price and timing of payment for dissenting shares
citations.quote: If the corporation and the shareholder agree that the shares are dissenting shares and agree upon the price of the shares, the dissenting shareholder is entitled to the agreed price with interest thereon at the legal rate on judgments from the date of the agreement. Any agreements fixing the fair market value of any dissenting shares as between the corporation and the holders thereof shall be filed with the secretary of the corporation. (b) Subject to the provisions of Section 1306, payment of the fair market value of dissenting shares shall be made within 30 days after the amount thereof has been agreed or within 30 days after any statutory or contractual conditions to the reorganization are satisfied, whichever is later, and in the case of certificated securities, subject to surrender of the certificates therefor, unless provided otherwise by agreement.

The two citations below are drawn from two separately, independently numbered sections (Cal. Corp. Code § 1300(a) and Cal. Corp. Code § 1303(a)-(b)). This document does not describe the separate mechanism (Section 1306, not independently verified for this document) under which unpaid fair market value can become a subordinated debt of the corporation if a distributions-restriction statute prevents payment, and it does not calculate the fair market value, the applicable legal rate of interest, or any specific payment date for any specific shares or transaction.

expectedJSON.body: If the corporation denies that particular shares are dissenting shares, or if the corporation and the shareholder cannot agree on fair market value, the shareholder demanding purchase (or any interested corporation) may file a complaint in the superior court of the proper county asking the court to determine whether the shares are dissenting shares, the shares' fair market value, or both -- or may intervene in a pending action raising the same questions. That complaint must be filed within six months after the date the corporation mailed its notice of outstanding-share approval, or the Section 1110(h) notice, to the shareholder; the statute states this deadline applies "but not thereafter." On the resulting trial, the court decides any disputed status issue first, and then determines fair market value itself or appoints one or more impartial appraisers to do so. Costs of that action, including reasonable compensation for court-appointed appraisers, are generally allocated as the court finds equitable; but if the appraised value exceeds the price the corporation had offered, the corporation must pay the costs, and the court has discretion to include attorneys' fees, expert-witness fees, and interest at the legal rate running from the date the shareholder complied with the demand-and-endorsement statutes, if the value the court awards for the shares turns out to be more than 125 percent of the price the corporation had offered.

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, action to determine dissenting-share status or fair market value, and its filing deadline
citations.quote: If the corporation denies that the shares are dissenting shares, or the corporation and the shareholder fail to agree upon the fair market value of the shares, then the shareholder demanding purchase of such shares as dissenting shares or any interested corporation, within six months after the date on which notice of the approval by the outstanding shares (Section 152) or notice pursuant to subdivision (h) of Section 1110 was mailed to the shareholder, but not thereafter, may file a complaint in the superior court of the proper county praying the court to determine whether the shares are dissenting shares or the fair market value of the dissenting shares or both or may intervene in any action pending on such a complaint.

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, allocation of litigation costs and fee-shifting when the court's appraisal exceeds the corporation's offer
citations.quote: The costs of the action, including reasonable compensation to the appraisers to be fixed by the court, shall be assessed or apportioned as the court considers equitable, but, if the appraisal exceeds the price offered by the corporation, the corporation shall pay the costs (including in the discretion of the court attorneys’ fees, fees of expert witnesses and interest at the legal rate on judgments from the date of compliance with Sections 1300, 1301 and 1302 if the value awarded by the court for the shares is more than 125 percent of the price offered by the corporation under subdivision (a) of Section 1301).

The two citations below are drawn from two separately, independently numbered sections (Cal. Corp. Code § 1304(a) and Cal. Corp. Code § 1305(e)). This document does not describe the separate rules in Section 1304(b)-(c) (joinder and consolidation of multiple dissenting shareholders' claims) or Section 1305(a)-(d) (the appraisers' reporting procedure and the form of judgment) in full, and does not determine whether a specific corporation's denial of dissenting-share status, or a specific valuation dispute, would in fact be litigated in a specific county's superior court, nor does it calculate any specific award, cost allocation, or the 125 percent threshold for any specific transaction.

expectedJSON.body: Shares can lose their status as dissenting shares -- and their holder can cease to be entitled to require the corporation to purchase them -- in any of several ways the statute lists: if the corporation abandons the reorganization (in which case the corporation must instead pay, on demand, the good-faith dissenting shareholder's necessary expenses and reasonable attorneys' fees incurred pursuing the dissenters'-rights process); if the shares are transferred before being submitted for endorsement, or are surrendered for conversion into another class under the articles; if the shareholder and corporation fail to agree on the shares' status or price and neither side files (or intervenes in) a court action within six months after the relevant notice was mailed; or if the shareholder withdraws the demand for purchase with the corporation's consent. Separately, the dissenters'-rights chapter limits what other remedies a shareholder who holds this cash-purchase right can pursue over the underlying transaction: a shareholder with a right under this chapter to demand cash for their shares generally has no right, at law or in equity, to attack the validity of the reorganization or short-form merger, or to have it set aside or rescinded -- except in an action testing whether the required vote to authorize or approve the transaction was legally obtained. That said, a holder of a share class whose own terms specifically set out what is to be paid on a reorganization is entitled to payment under those terms.

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, events that cause shares to lose their status as dissenting shares
citations.quote: Dissenting shares lose their status as dissenting shares and the holders thereof cease to be dissenting shareholders and cease to be entitled to require the corporation to purchase their shares upon the happening of any of the following: (a) The corporation abandons the reorganization. Upon abandonment of the reorganization, the corporation shall pay on demand to any dissenting shareholder who has initiated proceedings in good faith under this chapter all necessary expenses incurred in such proceedings and reasonable attorneys’ fees.

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, dissenters' rights as the shareholder's limited remedy against the reorganization itself
citations.quote: No shareholder of a corporation who has a right under this chapter to demand payment of cash for the shares held by the shareholder shall have any right at law or in equity to attack the validity of the reorganization or short-form merger, or to have the reorganization or short-form merger set aside or rescinded, except in an action to test whether the number of shares required to authorize or approve the reorganization have been legally voted in favor thereof; but any holder of shares of a class whose terms and provisions specifically set forth the amount to be paid in respect to them in the event of a reorganization or short-form merger is entitled to payment in accordance with those terms and provisions or, if the principal terms of the reorganization are approved pursuant to subdivision (b) of Section 1202, is entitled to payment in accordance with the terms and provisions of the approved reorganization.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of both the actual triggers for losing dissenting-share status and the actual limits this chapter places on other remedies -- not a claim about which state's law would apply to a specific corporation, and not a claim that dissenters' rights are always a shareholder's exclusive remedy in every jurisdiction. The two citations below are drawn from two separately, independently numbered sections (Cal. Corp. Code § 1309 and Cal. Corp. Code § 1312(a)). This document does not restate Section 1312(b)-(c) in full (the separate rule, and burden of proof, that applies when one party to the reorganization directly or indirectly controls another party to it), and it does not determine whether a specific shareholder's shares have in fact lost dissenting-share status, or whether a specific challenge to a specific transaction falls within the narrow vote-legality exception this section preserves.
